title: Days Until Next Event Using LEAD
description: For each scheduled event, show the event name, its date, the **next event's date** (using LEAD), and the **number of days until the next event**. The last event in the sequence should show NULL for both columns.
schema_sql: CREATE TABLE events (event_id INT, event_name VARCHAR(100), event_date DATE, venue VARCHAR(100)); INSERT INTO events VALUES (1,'Q1 All-Hands','2026-01-15','Main Hall'),(2,'Product Launch','2026-02-03','Auditorium'),(3,'Board Meeting','2026-02-20','Conference Room A'),(4,'Q2 Planning','2026-03-10','Main Hall'),(5,'Tech Summit','2026-03-28','Convention Center'),(6,'Mid-Year Review','2026-06-15','Conference Room B'),(7,'Q3 All-Hands','2026-07-20','Main Hall'),(8,'Annual Gala','2026-11-05','Grand Ballroom');
solution_sql: SELECT event_name, event_date, LEAD(event_date) OVER (ORDER BY event_date) AS next_event_date, LEAD(event_date) OVER (ORDER BY event_date) - event_date AS days_until_next FROM events ORDER BY event_date

test_cases.description: 8 events each with next_event_date and days_until_next. Annual Gala (last) shows NULL for both.

hints: LEAD(event_date) OVER (ORDER BY event_date) returns the event_date from the very next row in the ordered sequence — no partitioning needed here.
Subtracting two DATE values in PostgreSQL returns an integer number of days; the last event has no next row so LEAD returns NULL.
explanation: LEAD() is the forward-looking complement to LAG() — it peeks at the next row's value. Without a PARTITION BY, it operates across all rows ordered by event_date globally. Subtracting dates in PostgreSQL yields days directly. Q1 All-Hands to Product Launch = 19 days. Annual Gala is last, so LEAD returns NULL for both next_event_date and days_until_next.
